questions.prompt: Best comparison-based sorting lower bound (worst case) is:
questions.feedback:
Answer: Ω(n log n)

Why:
Comparison sorts need ≥ log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case.

Common mistake:
Citing only Ω(n).

Takeaway:
n! permutations ⇒ Ω(n log n) decision-tree height.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra’s algorithm assumes edge weights are:
questions.feedback:
Answer: Non-negative weights

Why:
Dijkstra finalizes distances; negatives can invalidate settled nodes.

Common mistake:
Assuming it works for arbitrary weights.

Takeaway:
w ≥ 0 ⇒ Dijkstra; negatives ⇒ Bellman-Ford.

questions.feedback:
Answer: False

Why:
Greedy needs a proof for global optimality; many counterexamples exist.

Common mistake:
Assuming greedy always works.

Takeaway:
Greedy is a technique, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Kruskal’s MST primarily uses which data structure family?
questions.feedback:
Answer: Union-Find

Why:
Kruskal adds lightest safe edges; Union-Find detects cycles/components.

Common mistake:
Naming only a heap or DFS.

Takeaway:
MST via sorted edges + Union-Find = Kruskal.

Common mistake:
Writing O(n²).

Takeaway:
Mergesort’s recurrence solves to Θ(n log n).

questions.prompt: Python: return True if sorted unique list a is a subset of set b.
questions.feedback:
Answer: set(a).issubset(b) or set(a) <= b

Why:
Set membership checks each element of a efficiently.

Common mistake:
Nested loops over lists.

Takeaway:
Use set operations for subset tests.
